terms.gloss: secondly, next (in a list of points)
evidence: Cic. Att. 6.3.1: prīmum quod vidētur esse honōs … deinde quod sōlum habeō praetōrium
Ter. Heaut. 3: Id prīmum dīcam: deinde quod vēnī ēloquar.
terms.comment: Latin counts its points prīmum … deinde … tum … postrēmō (or dēnique), and may repeat deinde for a third point. Its plain sense is “then, next” in time (see then).

evidence: Cic. Planc. 50 (Lewis & Short): prīmum, ut honōre dignus essem, maximē semper labōrāvī; secundō, ut existimārer; tertium …
terms.comment: Lewis & Short calls it rare: Cicero once, Phaedrus with prīmō. Later it is also “for the second time”.

terms.grammar: neuter of alter, as a noun
terms.comment: Where there are only two points, alter is “the second”: ūnum … alterum …, the one … the other (see another).

phrases.latin: prīmum est dēvium, deinde ab Autrōniō et cēterīs quadriduī, deinde sine tē.
phrases.english: Firstly, it’s off the road; secondly, it’s four days from Autronius and the rest; and thirdly, it’s without you.

phrases.latin: Id prīmum dīcam: deinde quod vēnī ēloquar.
phrases.english: I’ll explain that first; then I’ll say what I’ve come for.

sources: Lewis & Short: deinde · Lewis & Short: secundo · Lewis & Short: alter
Cic. Att. 3.7.1, 6.3.1 and Ter. Heaut. 3 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
